items.title: The since-clause can stand on either side

states.label: Since-clause first
states.sm: Talu ona ʻou sau ʻou te leʻi maua se mea lelei.
states.en: Since I came, I have not got anything good.

states.label: Since-clause last
states.sm: ʻOu te leʻi maua se mea lelei talu ona ʻou sau.
states.en: I have not got anything good since I came.

items.caption: The order changes and the meaning does not. The clause after *ona* usually has no tense particle of its own.

items.title: Which tool sets the time?

bins.label: An event packed into a le-phrase

items.sm: Talu ona ʻou alu ʻou te leʻi maua se mea fou.
items.en: Since I left, I have not got anything new.
items.why: *Talu* counts from the event in its complement clause.

items.sm: Ina ʻua malama le taeao, sā sau le pasi ʻenaʻena.
items.en: When the morning broke, the brown bus came.
items.why: The when-word opens the clause naming the event that turns the situation.

items.sm: Sā māfatia le tama ina ʻua malama le taeao.
items.en: The boy was exhausted when the morning broke.
items.why: The when-clause follows the main clause here.

items.sm: ʻO le sau o le pasi, e ʻāmata ai le malaga.
items.en: When the bus comes, the journey begins.
items.why: The fronted le-phrase names the bus coming, and *ai* in the other clause points back to it.

items.intro: Choose the construction that times the rest of each printed sentence.

items.title: Read how often

cells.note: The frequency word stands behind the verb inside the le-phrase.
The distributive number phrase comes before the time noun.
The number phrase follows the time noun here.

items.caption: The frequency word follows its verb. The distributive form works on a number inside a noun phrase; it is not a free-standing word for every.
